Messages.Author: Montri Chew
Messages.Body:
(The post below was captured from America Online - WotC is the official Wizards
of the Coast representative on America Online)

>Subj: Re:Jyhad Card Backs
>Date: 95-04-28 00:50:26 EDT
>From: WotC
>
>Backing A New Look
>Wizards of the Coast to Alter Card Backs in Vampire Game
>
>Renton, Wash. (April 26, 1995)-After reviewing customer comments, Wizards of
>the Coast, Inc. has decided to change all card backs in the newly named
>Vampire: The Eternal Struggle (V: TES) Deckmaster game. When the game-
>formerly titled Jyhad- debuts this summer, the cards will have the game's
>snake "biohazard" symbol and the new name on a green marble background. The
>old card backs featured the word Jyhad on green marble. "Changing the card
>backs doesn't affect how the game is played. Although you'll be able to see
>the back of the tail card in your opponent's hand and the top vampire in the
>crypt, you won't know what the cards are," says Matthew Burke, V: TES Project
>Coordinator. "Changing the card backs doesn't make Jyhad cards obsolete."
>
>The Duelists' Convocation will allow both Jyhad and V: TES cards in
>tournament play. Under Convocation rules, players will be able to use any
>combination of card backs during tournaments. The creator of the card game,
>Richard Garfield, agrees with using the two sets in tournaments. "I think
>the Duelists' Convocation rules allowing the use of both card backs goes a
>long way toward making the [Jyhad and V: TES] cards compatible," says
>Garfield.
>
>Wizards of the Coast realizes that by allowing both cards in tournaments,
>some players will take advantage of the different card backs and use some of
>one design to mark their cards. The Duelists' Convocation plans to crack
>down on dishonest competitors. "We will instruct Judges to look for this
>sort of behavior during tournaments. If the Judge finds a player is cheating
>by marking cards, the Judge will interpret this as a declaration of
>forfeiture," says Steve Bishop, Director of the Duelists' Convocation.
>
>Besides changing the card backs, Wizards of the Coast is also adjusting the
>game's rules. "We rewrote and reformatted the rules for easier reading," says
>Burke. "We also have added new variant rules to increase the pace of the
>game for those who want to play quick sessions." The new version of the
>rules will appear in instructions that accompany each V: TES starter deck and
>also in a new player's guide, Darkness Unveiled. The guide is due out this
>September.
>
>One month prior to that, the game's first expansion set, Dark Sovereigns,
>will be released. More than 100 cards will make up this expansion, which
>explores the rich myths and folklore of vampires in Europe. The set will
>also introduce players to new vampires and new categories of vampires.
>
>Earlier this year, Wizards of the Coast signed a contract with White Wolf,
>Inc. to change Jyhad's name to Vampire: The Eternal Struggle after
>recognizing that the game's title wasn't always distinguishable as vampiric.
>The card game, in which players are vampires fighting an ancient war, is
>based on White Wolf's storytelling game Vampire: The Masquerade.

The customer comments that the press release alluded to was based on a post by
WotC on AOL a few weeks ago which requested people to send comments to Wizards
of the Coast regarding 4 card backs options for the Vampire: The
Eternal Struggle - keep all the card backs the same, change only the
crypt card backs, change all card backs but pretend to make the two
editions playable in tournaments, and change all card backs and don't
pretend to make the two editions playable in tournaments. I feel it
was a charade put on by Wizards of the Coast since they didn't even
bother to put that survey out anywhere else on the net that I know of
(Internet, CompuServe, & GeNIE).

With regards to tournaments, I think most tournament organizers will
not put up with the potential cheating problem and will simply ban
decks which mixes the two editions. Jyhad will indeed become obselete
regardless of what Wizards of the Coast wants us to believe.

Oh well. I guess I should thank Wizards of the Coast since I'll be
saving quite a bit of money now that I won't be buying Vampire: The
Eternal Struggle (and probably any future Deckmaster games). I've
pretty much lost all respect for WotC because of the way they've
handled this issue. What really galled me is the way they kept
changing their decision (the last previous one was keeping the library
card backs the same) and then resorting to a public relation subtefuge
to justify what they've apparently wanted to do all along.

>(Internet, CompuServe, & GeNIE).

That survey posted to AOL was in no way intended to be an exhaustive survey
of what people though about the card back issue. It was posted to AOL because
the AOL NetRep had concerns on the issue, so *he* went ahead and polled the
people in the forum he was covering. There is nothing wrong with this, but
it should not be construed as an attempt to base the decision solely on
AOL feedback. The decision was based on feedback from all sorts of sources,
both on and off the net.

>With regards to tournaments, I think most tournament organizers will
>not put up with the potential cheating problem and will simply ban
>decks which mixes the two editions. Jyhad will indeed become obselete
>regardless of what Wizards of the Coast wants us to believe.

The Convocation rules will explicitly allow mixing Jyhad and V:TES card backs.
Banning one or the other in a sanctioned tournaments is a good way to put the
tournament on the fast track to being thrown out. Obviously unofficial
tournaments can do what they want, but hopefully people will realize that
it's actually difficult to blatantly mark your deck with mixed card backs.

>What really galled me is the way they kept
>changing their decision (the last previous one was keeping the library
>card backs the same) and then resorting to a public relation subtefuge
>to justify what they've apparently wanted to do all along.

The decision was in flux precisely because of customer feedback. The
"subterfuge" you refer to was not an attempt to assess overall customer
input, just one NetRep acting on his own.

Semprini <ska...@u.washington.edu> wrote:
>Is it just me, or can the same logic that was applied in making decks be
>All Alpha or No Alpha in Magic tournaments be applicable here? They say
>that it will be allowed... suuuuuuure. Did they really think through the
>compatibility issues here? Did they really think they can convince
>judges to take the time to check EVERYBODY's DECK???

No, we do not expect judges to check everybody's deck, though they can do
so if they want. We expect players to police each other, and to only call
the judges over if they seriously suspect systematic marking of the deck.
Also, as the press release points out, it's difficult to marking your deck
with different card backs without your opponent figuring out what you're
doing, and thus neutralizing the advantage.

There is no "all alpha or no alpha" rule in the Jyhad tournament rules
that are forthcoming. Judges are required to allow people to mix the
two types of cards.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Jeremy York <bea...@netcom.com> wrote:
>Even if I wasn't intending to cheat, if I know my cards
>well and recall that Dancin Dana, Bianca, and Dre in my crypt
>were the only ones with card back X, I *definitely* gain info
>by seeing the top card in the crypt...

And so does everyone else, after a game or two. Also, it seems to me that
knowing certain vampire are coming up is only an advantage if there is a wide
spread of ages and/or abilities among the vampires in your crypt, which
face it, doesn't happen much in tournament decks. That degree of randomness
is simply more than your average tournament player is willing to tolerate.

>So a different card back means giving the player with the
>mixed deck a slight advantage. But, I'll remind you, way back
>in late '93 Wizards was thinking about this issue (for Magic), and
>Garfield's inclination was to say that this doesn't make that much
>difference. He originally wanted to have each expansion set have a
>different back design - this way, if you wanted to say "I don't like to
>play against decks with Antiquities", you'd know whether your
>opponent was complying or not. And for sportsmanlike players,
>the knowledge gained this way doesn't mean much. I'd agree with
>this up to a point for Jyhad/V:tES, but the Crypt is the main
>difference to me. As a better example than what I gave above, if I
>have six cards of back X and six of Y in my crypt, and during play
>have drawn 4 X and one Y, and note that the top card in the crypt is
>an X, then I know that it is one of two Vamps.

That's pretty much our take on the issue, yes. But the crypt thing isn't
even seen as that big of a deal.

>What about cards that have changed in power, applicability, etc,
>due to re-wordings?
>There are two approaches to this. One is the WotC Magic way,
>in which an old card is to be played as written no matter how
>broken (unless an official errata has been issued)...
>The other approach is the Steve Jackson INWO approach, which is
>to play any old cards as if they had the new wording...

Remember, the second approach is the one we would prefer to take, but taking
it requires a reliable way of informing people as to what the latest card
texts *are*. In Magic, it has taken far too long to provide such a way
of distributing the information, but it will be coming out in the forseeable
future. We probably won't have such a system for Jyhad/V:TES right away,
but it should take a lot less time to accomplish it there than it has
with Magic.

Exactly what history are we revising? Matt's comments about what policy
he was planning to set for the card backs? That doesn't strike me as
a very definite plan. What had been posted previously was tentative plans
for what to do about the card backs. The recent press release is definite
plans on what to do about them. What's basically going on here (without
pointing fingers) is that people want us to post all sorts of information
on what we're going to do before we have a final policy, and then trying
to hold us to those tentative plans. You can't have it both ways, folks.
We can't be forced into making a final policy just because we choose to
post speculative plans to the net; speculating one thing and then ultimately
deciding to do another is not revisionist history, it is the evolution of
a business plan, with some public insight into what's going on in our heads.

>> ...Please show some respect for those who find the word 'jyhad' offensive.

>How about showing respect for those people who find "magic" offensive? I
>don't see them changing the card backs of Mt$ when they revised the rules?

This whole "jyhad is offensive" thread is way out of hand, and is not the
primary reason for changing the name of the game, or the card backs.
The primary reason is that Jyhad was not reaching the target audience, because
the target audience had no idea what the product was.

>How about showing respect for the people who have purchased significant
>amounts of Jyhad cards and have put a lot of time and effort into promoting

>the game [like me]? IMHO, WotC is fucking over the older players...

How is expanding the market of players going to harm the older players?
It's not like we're turning it into a completely new game, or shutting people
out from using Jyhad cards. The change had to happen, for the benefit of
the overall game.

PLEASE EVERYONE. The word Jyhad is not being used in a derogatory
fashion. If people take it that way, they are finding insult where
there is none. Im not saying insults are not possible - but it can be
taken too far. The INTENT and CONTEXT are as important as the word
itself - and it is quite clear once one looks at the game and the
rulebook what the intent is.

The word jihad, in the English language, has the meaning "a crusade
for a principle or belief" (Webster's). Words are (except for
corporate trademarks :) ) able to be used by anyone who wants. This is
as silly as banning the word "genocide" because of Hitler, the word
"slavery" because of antebellum U.S. culture, etc. "Slavery" has
existed all over the word, as has genocide, and yes even jihads. The
word is Arabic in origin, but if youre speaking English (which you
were) it is legal to apply it to any "crusade for a principle or
belief", which is exactly why it was chosen by White Wolf for Vampire:
The Masquerade, and why the WotC game was so named.

Words are not inherently bad or good. Their USAGE is. Their usage in
this context refers to a war waged by vampires among themselves.

If any vampires are offended, let them call WotC. Otherwise, I think
the idea of the term being used offensively is crap.

But why are people insisting on not even *trying* to play the game with
mixed card backs? Having watched several games of Dark Sovereigns playtesting,
in which the DS cards were these little white rectangles of paper and thus
blatantly obvious, it just didn't seem to be any kind of advantage to know
that you had a DS card coming up vs. a Jyhad card coming up. Great, so you
you know you have a Sovereigns card coming up; so do your opponents.

I would suggest that anyone concerned about the mixed card backs try a
little experiment. Find a bunch of basic lands from Magic (they are the
same size as Jyhad cards, even), and proxy some amount of your Jyhad deck.
Play a few games and see if it really helps to know that you have one
of the proxy cards coming up, instead of one of your Jyhad cards, and see
if it really makes a difference in your play strategies. In all of the
inhouse playtesting for Dark Sovereigns, nobody ever decided that knowing
whether they were getting a Dark Sovereign or Jyhad card was coming up
was a particular advantage. It certainly wasn't any more of an advantage
than just building the deck out of 10 cards or so.

Or, if you have more Jyhad lying around than you know what to do with, use
spare cards with they "JYHAD" on the back blacked out, instead of using
basic lands. The visual cue of a card coming up will be less obvious,
making the test more accurate.

sizes and printing styles, but assuming there's a reasonable blend of the
two card backs, it's difficult to try and cheat based on the backs. Granted,

different from your functional cards. In Jyhad, the resources and the
functional cards are basically in different decks, so this concern doesn't
really apply. The other reason to mix alphas is to mark a few key cards to

cards right now, or do something to build up what you have in play. Since
you know in Jyhad that you're probably going to draw the top card of your
library within the next turn, and since the wild type of decks that this
alpha marking helps with don't exist in Jyhad, this is not really an
issue either.

Messages.Author: Jeremy York
Messages.Body:
An example from experience that different card backs in a large
deck don't make that much difference - Galactic Empires. It
is trivial to tell, at a glance, the difference between a
alpha/beta card and a Primary edition/expansion card. This
is because the older cards were on a linen finish stock; the
texture of this stock is easily recognizable.

Has this made any appreciable difference in any game of GE
I've ever played (even though *all* of us were playing with
mixed decks)? Not that I was able to notice.

The example someone gave of have a Jyhad deck with only
Necromancy cards with a V:tES back was a good one. If you
don't have a decent vamp with that discipline in play, you're
not going to discard a potentially useful card just in hopes
of getting something good. The opposite case holds true - you
know that your necromancy cards would come in very handy, so
you ditch something, anything, just to be able to draw it.

BUT it doesn't need to be that way if you make a point of
being a good sport. In Magic, I used to play a lot with decks
that had all editions of the cards, including alphas. To
offset any unfair advantage this might give me, I always kept
my pool of land cards totally mixed up. If I grab a handful
of Swamps for a deck, I might get one-third alphas. Similarly
with all of my commons.

This way I made sure that my deck was sporting - seeing that alpha on
top of my deck didn't tell me "aha, that's either my ancestral
recall or my winter orb" because it might have been an Island
or a Llanowar elf, too.

So don't use only Necromancy cards from a V:tES expansion in
a Jyhad deck. Buy or trade for a few regular V:tES cards, and
replace a bunch of your commons, indiscriminantly, with the equivalent
new edition card. Advantage zapped, no longer an issue.

"I can't expect my opponents to do the same" you say. Well,
maybe not, but it's an issue of sportsmanship. A good sport
tries to play in a way that's fair even if that fairness
is not universally practiced. And again, I say, if I play
against people who I think cheat or abuse the game system
to their advantage, I confront them about it and stop playing
with them.

OK, this isn't exactly a defence or condemnation of the card back switch
made by Wizards of the Coast. However, I've read a few comments
concerning the name 'Jyhad' which I REALLY have to respond to, as people
are brushing off the 'offensive to others' argument as specious, a
marketing ploy, or what have.

If nothing else, I definitely agree with this particular point. Jyhad,
used in the manner it is in both White Wolf products and in the CCG
produced by WotC, IS offensive. Jihad, or Jyhad is an arabic term which
does NOT mean war, or conflict, as so many people in the Western world
are quick to believe, but simply means 'struggle'. A 'jihad' in
mainstream Islam SELDOM refers to an armed conflict or a 'war against the
infidels', but instead to a spiritual struggle. Usually.

Unfortunately, the Western media (as it is wont to do) has picked up the
term and completely misapplied in numerous ways. While certain terrorist
groups (Islamic Jihad, for one) have taken the name, this is no different
than a group which calls itself Church of the True Christianity, which
then proceeds to blow away small children (they don't exist, but its for
the sake of example). Of course, since most North Americans aren't
exposed to Islamic belief systems, and are far more familiar with
Christianity, its easy to assume that a Jihad is something dark and nasty.

Sadly, this term has even found itself misapplied in the RPG industry...I
was moderately upset with White Wolf that they used it to denote the
continual struggle for dominance amongst the Vampire Clans, although they
at least were correct in the denotion of it as a 'struggle'. Nor was I
pleased with Wizards of the Coast when they had a 'Jihad' card in Arabian
Nights which depicting an armed host thundering across the plains. Use of
this term in such a way only perpetuates an already dangerous stereotype.
When 'Jyhad', the CCG came out, I was upset yet again...and now I'm
rather impressed that WotC has changed the name.

Note, however, that I'm not exactly sure what effect this will have on
gameplay, however, and I can't say that I think this decision was
entirely a good one. However, to dismiss the argument that 'Jyhad is
offensive' by saying it is not relevent is not exactly fair.

Just my Canadian .02.

I take my cultural studies seriously...and of course, my field in Anthro is

How did you arrive at the converse conclusion? That we'd prefer to have
the card backs changed? And dismissing the change as meaningless because
it provides no 'advantage' overlooks two important points, which are
principally behind my (and I feel many other's) dismay at this change.

[Life story mode engaged. Music swells. Lights dim.]

In high school my friends and I were all rabid card players. We played
many games which required standard decks, such as Bridge, Cribbage, Hearts,
and 9-2-5 (the *best* 3 person game for standard decks). We also played
Pinochle, which uses a 48 card deck consisting of two of all the 9s through
As from all four suits. We would usually take two of our normal decks
and just take the relevant cards from the red and blue decks and combine
them. I have probably played around twice as many 1500 point series of
Pinochle, using 50:50 mixed-back decks, as games of Jyhad.
In all that time, I don't think the split decks gave anyone much of an
advantage. Once in a great while you would be able to tell if someone
had a card of a suit or not (by seeing that they had nothing but blue
cards) but this was neither frequent nor important. But the split decks
*were* unsatisfactory, and eventually we shelled out the three bucks for
a proper Pinochle deck with just one back.

First, it added a complication to the game that was not in the rules.
It changed the way you count cards -- you can count by back as well as
suit and rank. In friendly play, we were usually too busy cracking jokes
to count cards at all (let alone this carefully) but when we wanted to, it
was not too hard to count them all. In a tournament with split decks,
I would absolutely count the cards by back, just because occasionally
it would net an extra 10 points to set a contract. If my opponents don't,
then I have a net advantage. If my opponents do, there's no net advantage.
But the character of the game is subtly and *significantly* changed, since
players have more information about their opponents cards as before.
Second, it was just plain ANNOYING. If we didn't have the pinochle
deck with us, we made do with two normal decks, amongst general mummerings
of 'gooberhead forgot the pinochle deck again...' Having two different
backs in the same deck was just not as aesthetically pleasing as having
a proper, single-backed deck. It was an unnecessary complication to the
game, and when we had the right deck we _always_ used it instead of the
mixed deck, even though the pinochle deck was all worn-out and sticky
while the mixed deck was made of two nice new decks.

And that's just with perfect 50:50 mixed decks, that everyone knew the
total contents of. With self-constructed decks, which nobody else knows
the contents of, the possible change in the game environment is greater
and will subtly, but significantly, change the way people play the game.
If mixed decks come into play, it will just become another thing serious
players will have to diligently keep track of. It will not have _too_
great an advantage, but since every marginal advantage counts in a
tournament setting, this means that all serious players will have to keep

>significant portion of the net.aware players seem to think it will). Yes,
>mixing card backs can be a useful tactic and at the very least can give you
>valuable information about what is coming up next in your deck. Here's a very
>good example: Let's say you have a Brujah rush combat deck and a sizable number
>of both sets of cards. You could make all your non-combat cards VtES backs and
>all your combat cards Jyhad backs. Now, I'm in combat and I see that my next
>card is a VtES back, I won't press and hope to draw a Strike card, because I
>KNOW that the next card isn't. I've been in this situation (should I press/
>maneuver and hope to draw a strike) several times recently [I've been playing
>Brujah quite a bit since Curt Adams claimed they couldn't beat S&B] and KNOWING
>whether the next card is playable in the current combat or not IS a big advantage.

You're going to have to do a lot better than this. I'm not much of a
Jyhad player, but if you were playing this deck, and the dividing line were
this clear (combat cards vs. noncombat cards), it would probably take a couple
of turns at most before I couldn't help but notice the pattern... and then
you would start getting hammered, because I would know how many combat cards
you had in your hand and whether or not you would be drawing one soon, and I
would start altering my attacks and tactics appropriately. I would wager a
lot of money that I could make a lot more use out of knowing the nature of
your whole hand _and_ your next card than you could do knowing only the
nature of your next card. And, since I'd be playing all Jyhad backs, you
would have no such information about my cards.

People, before you start thinking about obvious marketing strategies,
think about this fact; if your opponent can figure out the pattern, your
opponent is getting much more added information than you're getting. You
know what your cards are once they're in your hand; he doesn't, unless you
use the card backs to telegraph that fact to him. In fact, if I were
playing in a tournament under the proposed rules, I think I'd play a mixed
deck with a totally random pattern of mixing (and chuckle softly when I
saw a V:tES card turn up in my deck), just to drive my opponent crazy and
take his attention off the game while he's trying to figure out a pattern
that doesn't exist. :-)

The only rule I might add would be a minimum-proportions rule--say, if
you're going to use a mixed deck, at least 25% of the cards have to come from
each set. With that many cards of one "marking", the pattern is likely to
be either obvious enough that the opponent will catch on quickly, or nebulous
enough that it won't be much help to anyone.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie

The name of Magic: the Gathering is not changing. Changing the packaging
on the boxes is just the sort of thing you do to keep a product fresh whenever
you upgrade it to a new edition. Jyhad is becoming Vampire: the Eternal
Struggle. The two games are perfectly compatible, but it *is* a different
product, and hence warrants a more extensive change in presentation than
a new edition of an existing product does. M:tG is still called M:tG, so there
is no reason to remove that from the card backs. Jyhad is now called V:TES,
so there's a very real reason to change the overall presentation.

Magic is doing far better than anyone could have ever dreamed of. Jyhad
was a disappointment, especially in projected markets outside of the gaming
industry. Thus there is no reason to overhaul Magic, and a very real reason
to overhaul Jyhad.

Jyhad is much more combination-dependent than Magic. In addition, most

Close but no cigar. Right on the definition of resource, but wrong on the
application to Jyhad.

In Jyhad, almost every card will serve as a resource for another in a good
deck. I need stealth to use my + bleed; I need + bleed to use my stealth.
I need Rush to use combat cards; I need combat cards to use Rush. I need
useful actions to tap out to use my Wakes; I need Wakes to tap out doing
useful actions. I need Disguised Weapon to pull surprises with my
weaponry; I need weaponry to usefully use my DW. I need presses for my
Thaumaturgy nukes, I need Thaumaturgy nukes to safely use presses. I need
Flashes for my Sewer Lid; I need ranged damage for my manuevers. Etc.,
etc., etc.

Nobody can figure out a good Jyhad marking scheme in a real game. You
have multiple opponents to track and they will probably have sophisticated
marking schemes which you will never see again. They can switch schemes
for every deck after every session, or, if that's too much work, every
time somebody cracks the code. I'll switch from marking my Rushes to
marking my presses.

Even if a deck is not marked, card counting will provide an edge. When
I've drawn all my Jyhad Wakes, I'll know a Jyhad card is something else -
most likely the stealth where I've drawn mostly VTES. Most people can
count their own decks, but almost nobody can count a whole table. In any
case, they won't know the relative composition of my deck, so seeing 3
Jyhad Wakes means much less to them than to me.

I think there's a lesson here. Intel had a public relations problem.
They had some chips with a minor defect which almost no one would
actually care about. By ignoring their customers they turned it into a
major corporate disaster. The funny thing is that when they finally
gave in, and let everyone exchange their "defective" chips for free,
only about 2% of their customers actually bothered. The whole thing
would have cost them virtually nothing, except that the stupid way they
handled it pissed people off, and now they are stuck with a warehouse
full of "old" chips which they have to write off.

So, what's my solution? Let anyone who wants to, mail in their Jyhad
cards to be exchanged for the identical VTES cards. They can play with
homogeneous backs, so they are happy. The cards cost you little, so you
are happy. As long as you make both card backs legal (as you are doing)
only a very few people will actually bother to send in their cards, so
it won't be a big job for you. And you won't have to deal with the PR
problem caused by a small group of loud voices.

(Besides, if enough people do mail them in, then the old Jyhad cards
will get scarce/valuable, and then you can resell them at a profit....)

Peace Tom,

Please, don't take this personnally (sp), it isn't. I believe that above
paragraph demonstrates just how little Jyhad you have played. As I previously
posted, using the discard phase is the single greatest thing that separates
the experience players from the newbies. A newbie _will_ hold all his/her
"good" cards and wait for a situation in which to play them. An experienced
player will recongnize that if you sit there will a "dead hand," no matter
how useful those cards may be in other circumstances, you will lose. Therefore
an experienced player _will_ discard often (I do). Everytime that I have
taught a new player, I have tried to stress the importance of the Discard Phase.
Unfortunately, ingrained Magic habits prevent new players from discarding
on a regular basis. Additionally, as Alan Kwan pointed out, a will constructed
deck has no problem with discarding regularly as the card you draw will be
no worse than (and most probably better than) the card you are discarding.
KNOWING that the next card on my library is valuable gives a significant
advantage during the discard phase. It can change a "skill decision" into
a "die roll" ("should I 'risk' a discard" vs. "luckily, I just happened to have
the card I need sitting on top of my deck"). The best designed decks take
discarding into account.

Sorry if you took this as a personal attack. Such was not intended. It was
only meant as a rebuttle to your argument.

The only way that WotC has a good chance of countering the negative perception
of the card back changes would be for them to put out the kind of effort
promoting the game they did when the originally came out. That is, put
Corey and Crew on tour with Jyhad (excuse me) Vampire tournaments, demo
games, etc.. If the group of existing players seems as alienated by the change
as this thread indicates, then the core players will not serve to market the
game. This means that WotC will have to try to augment or rebuild the core.
Which they have done before--Jyhad originally had NO followers.

Personally, I have taught several dozen people to play JYHAD at ELYSEUM in
San Jose, and at conventions. I am less interested in doing so now, because
of the card back change. I am not going to buy new VTES cards (I have enough
JYHAD cards to last a lifetime), and I am very wary of the new expansion.

WotC may have sold 180 Million cards, but a lot of these are STILL sitting
on store shelves. The first print run of JYHAD/VTES has NOT been purchased
by end-users, but is STUCK in the retail channel. The store owners I know
(and I know dozens across the U.S.) are going to be VERY CAREFUL about their
orders for VTES. They'll get SOME, but since they have boxes of JYHAD still
sitting on their shelves, they don't really need additional stock. The
expansion will do better, as the inconvenience of the new card back might be
worth the effort if the cards are worthwhile, but again, the store owners
will be cautious.

Even more than our complaints here, the fact that JYHAD sits unsold in game
stores ALL OVER THE UNITED STATES indicates that VTES may not be a viable
game in today's CCG marketplace.
